title: Aggregate Functions
subtitle: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, GROUP BY, and HAVING
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: You need to answer questions like 'How many orders per user?' or 'What is the average product price by category?' — questions about groups of rows, not individual rows.
whyItExists.solution: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) collapse multiple rows into a single value. GROUP BY splits rows into groups first, then aggregates each group separately.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any summary question: totals, averages, counts, extremes. Dashboards, reports, analytics.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use GROUP BY when you need individual row details — it collapses rows. For per-row calculations alongside aggregates, use window functions.

explainModes.beginner: COUNT(*) counts how many rows. SUM(price) adds up all prices. AVG(price) is the average. MIN and MAX find the smallest and largest. GROUP BY 'city' groups users by city first, then counts each group.
explainModes.simple: Aggregate functions: COUNT(*) — total rows, COUNT(col) — non-null values, SUM(col), AVG(col), MIN(col), MAX(col). GROUP BY col — one group per unique value; each group gets one output row. SELECT col, AGG(x) FROM table GROUP BY col. HAVING — filter groups (like WHERE but after GROUP BY). Every non-aggregate column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY.
explainModes.standard: Logical execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after grouping. COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs. COUNT(col) counts only non-NULL values — different results if column has NULLs! AVG ignores NULLs too. GROUP BY with ROLLUP (some databases) adds subtotals.
explainModes.technical: GROUP BY implements the relational algebra group-by operation. The engine chooses hash aggregation (build hash table per group) or sort-based aggregation (sort by GROUP BY key, then aggregate runs). Hash is usually faster for small groups, sort for large sorted datasets. Aggregates in HAVING can reference non-SELECT aggregates. GROUP BY ALL (some databases) groups by all non-aggregate SELECT columns implicitly.
explainModes.deepDive: FILTER clause (PostgreSQL, SQLite 3.30+): COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE condition) — conditional aggregate without a CASE expression. Ordered-set aggregates: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY price) — median. Hypothetical-set aggregates: RANK(value) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY col). ANY_VALUE(col) — pick any value from a group (deterministic, fast). Statistics aggregates: STDDEV, VARIANCE. GROUPING SETS, CUBE, ROLLUP for multi-dimensional aggregation.

content.code:
-- Count products per category
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM products
GROUP BY category;

-- Average price per category
SELECT category, ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY avg_price DESC;

-- Total orders per user
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(total) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

-- HAVING: filter groups (like WHERE but for groups)
-- Users who spent more than 1000 total
SELECT user_id, SUM(total) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING total_spent > 1000;

-- WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping
-- HAVING filters groups AFTER grouping
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM products
WHERE stock > 50           -- filter rows first
GROUP BY category
HAVING product_count >= 2; -- then filter groups

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: They are identical — WHERE and HAVING both filter rows
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY
HAVING filters rows before grouping; WHERE filters after
WHERE is used with aggregates; HAVING is for regular columns
questions.explanation: Execution order: FROM → WHERE (filter rows) → GROUP BY (create groups) → HAVING (filter groups) → SELECT. WHERE cannot reference aggregate functions because aggregation hasn't happened yet. HAVING can reference aggregates because it runs after GROUP BY.

faq.q: Why does COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) give different results?
faq.a: COUNT(*) counts every row, including rows where the column is NULL. COUNT(column) counts only rows where that specific column is NOT NULL. If your column has 3 NULL values in 10 rows: COUNT(*) = 10, COUNT(column) = 7.

faq.q: Can I use a WHERE condition and a HAVING condition in the same query?
faq.a: Yes! Use WHERE to filter individual rows first (before grouping), then HAVING to filter the resulting groups. Example: WHERE price > 100 filters out cheap products, then GROUP BY category, HAVING COUNT(*) > 2 keeps only categories with more than 2 remaining products.

examples: SELECT DATE(created_at), COUNT(*) AS signups FROM users GROUP BY DATE(created_at) — daily signup chart
SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS sold FROM orders GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY sold DESC LIMIT 5 — top 5 products
SELECT AVG(rating) FROM reviews WHERE product_id = ? — average rating for a product
